unit.title: Draw and interpret sketch and simple drawing

summary: This Level 3 unit teaches you to read and use engineering and fabrication drawings, and to make clear sketches of your own. You will learn drawing types and drawing control, lines, views and projection, sections, dimensions, scales and tolerances, steel section sizes and notes, and weld symbols. You will also sketch existing work on site, turn drawings into cutting lists and weld schedules, check finished work against the drawing, and brief a team on a drawing.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). A drawing is how a designer tells the workshop exactly what to make: the shape, every size, the material, the welds and the finish. A sketch is how you pass information the other way: from a site or an existing part back to the workshop or the office. If a drawing is misread, or a sketch is unclear, the job is made wrong, however good the welding.

At Level 3 you read drawings for the whole team. You check that a drawing set is complete and current before work starts, turn it into cutting lists and weld schedules, raise queries, brief the team and check the finished work against it. You also make dimensioned sketches on site, clear enough for someone else to work from.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 3 trainees at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and welders, fitters and supervisors who work from drawings and produce sketches.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Work only from current drawings; read the title block and revision table; withdraw old copies; return marked-up changes.
Understand orthographic views in first and third angle projection, sections, hidden detail, centre lines and break lines.
Use the written dimensions, work with scales, understand datum and chain dimensions, and work out tolerance limits.
Read steel section sizes, material grades, finishes, hole notes and abbreviations.
Read the type, size, side, length and pitch of each weld, and the extra signs for site welds, welds all round and finishing.
Make neat, dimensioned freehand orthographic and isometric sketches of parts and existing work, with a title block.
Produce cutting lists and weld schedules, set out joints, query errors and check finished work against the drawing.
Brief the team on a drawing and help team members who find a drawing hard to read.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on drawing control, drawing types, projection and views, lines and sections, dimensions and tolerances, scale, weld symbols, sections and materials, notes, sketching and using drawings on the job.
A **written paper** with short answers (names, abbreviations and calculated sizes) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two team practicals**: surveying a fabricated item at the Centre and producing a checked set of orthographic and isometric sketches with weld symbols and a cutting list; and reading a fabrication drawing to make a cutting list and weld schedule, setting out a corner joint full size, and inspecting a sample frame against the drawing.

blocks.note: Short answers ask for exact names: bill of materials, section, hatching, development, dimension line, drawing register, other side, circular hollow section, universal beam. Learn the Key terms and the abbreviations table.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Types of drawing and drawing control

head: Drawing or document
What it shows
Who uses it
rows: The whole item or structure, how the parts fit together and where each one goes, with overall sizes
A sub-assembly (for example one gate leaf) and how its parts are joined
One part, with every size, hole, edge preparation and note needed to make it
A member or assembly as the workshop makes it, with its piece mark, welds and holes
Where each piece mark goes on site and how it is fixed
The flat shape of a sheet-metal part before it is bent or rolled
Parts list or bill of materials (BOM)
Each part's number, description, material, size and quantity
Each piece to be cut, its section, length and number
Each joint, its weld type, size and side, and the procedure
Written requirements: materials, standards, finish, testing

blocks.p: The **title block**, usually in the bottom right-hand corner, identifies the drawing. Read it before anything else.

ul: Drawing number and title; sheet number (for example sheet 2 of 5)
Revision letter or number, and its date
Scale, and the projection symbol (first or third angle)
Units (usually 'All dimensions in mm') and the general tolerance
Material and finish, if they apply to the whole drawing
Who drew, checked and approved it, and the client and job
Each time a drawing is changed it gets a new **revision** letter (A, B, C...) or number.
The **revision table** (revision block) lists each revision, the date, what was changed and who approved it.
On the drawing, the changed area is usually marked with a **cloud** (a wavy outline) or a small triangle with the revision letter.
When a new revision arrives, read the revision table and check whether any parts already cut, drilled or welded are affected.

head: Part of the system
What happens
rows: A list kept with the drawings, giving every drawing number with its latest revision and issue date. Check it before work starts.
New revisions are issued to everyone who holds a copy; the issue is recorded, so the office knows who must get the next one.
Old copies are collected and stamped VOID or SUPERSEDED, or destroyed, so no one can work from them.
Changes agreed on site are marked in red on a working copy, signed and dated, and returned to the office so the master drawing can be updated.
Drawings updated to show what was actually built, kept for the client's records and future repairs.

blocks.note: Many shops now view drawings on a tablet or phone. Fine detail, such as a decimal point or a small weld symbol, is easy to misread on a small screen. Zoom in on every size, check you are looking at the latest revision, and never measure from a screen.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Check the register and work only from current copies.
Remove old copies from the work area.
Record agreed changes on the working copy and return it.
Send queries and errors to the supervisor or drawing office in writing, and record the answers.

head: Line
How it looks
What it shows
rows: Dimension lines, extension (projection) lines, leader lines, hatching
Hidden edges and outlines, such as a hole through a block seen from the side
Centre lines, lines of symmetry, pitch circles
Chain thin, thick at the ends
Chain line with heavy ends and arrows
A cutting plane, showing where a section is taken and which way you look
A straight line with a zigzag in it
A break: part of a long member's length is left out to fit the sheet
Adjacent parts, or the other position of a moving part

blocks.p: An **orthographic** drawing shows an object in separate flat views, each looking straight at one side: usually the **front view** (front elevation), the **plan** (looking down from above) and an **end view** (end elevation). Choose as the front view the side that shows the most about the shape. Draw only as many views as are needed: a flat plate with holes needs one view and a note of its thickness.

blocks.h: First angle and third angle projection

head: Point
First angle
Third angle
rows: To the right of the front view
To the left of the front view
Each view is drawn on the far side of the object from where it is seen
Each view is drawn on the same side it is seen from
The symbol (a cone shown in two views)
The circles are drawn beside the large end of the cone
The circles are drawn beside the small end of the cone

blocks.p: You will meet both in Jamaica, as drawings come from designers trained in different systems and from overseas suppliers. **Always look for the projection symbol** before you read the views. If you read a drawing in the wrong projection, you can put holes, brackets or bevels on the wrong face, or make a whole batch as mirror images.

A sloping face looks shorter than it really is in the normal views. An **auxiliary view** looks straight at the sloping face, so its true shape and the true positions of holes on it can be shown and dimensioned.

ul: A **section** is a view drawn as if the part has been cut through, to show its inside shape.
A **cutting plane line**, labelled for example A–A, shows where the cut is made; the arrows at its ends show the direction you look to see the section.

Cut surfaces are **hatched** with thin lines, usually at 45° and evenly spaced. Two parts that touch are hatched in different directions (or at different spacing) so you can see they are separate parts. The same part has the same hatching in every view.
Bolts, nuts, pins, shafts and thin webs or ribs cut along their length are **not** hatched, so they are easy to recognise.
Very thin sections, such as sheet or gaskets, may be shown solid black.

Types: full section (cut right through), half section (one quarter removed, for symmetrical parts), part or broken-out section (a small area), revolved and removed sections (a slice through a member, drawn on or beside it).

blocks.p: **Isometric** and **oblique** drawings show the object in three dimensions in one picture. They help people who find orthographic views hard to read, and they are often used on GA drawings and in sketches. Sizes are still taken from the orthographic views.

blocks.note: If a view does not make sense, find the same feature in the other views. Every line in one view lines up with a feature in the view next to it.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Dimension line:** a thin line with an arrowhead at each end, with the size written on it.
**Extension (projection) lines:** thin lines from the feature to the dimension line, with a small gap at the object.
**Leader line:** a thin line with an arrow or dot, pointing from a note to a feature.
Sizes are in millimetres unless the drawing says otherwise; the units are not written after each size.
Diameters have Ø in front (Ø22); radii have R (R10).

head: Method
What it looks like
What to watch
rows: Every size measured from one datum edge or line
The best method for accuracy: errors do not add up
Each size measured from the feature before
Small errors add up along the row; measure from the datum where you can
One line of sizes from a datum, each written at its feature
Same benefit as datum dimensioning, in less space
A size in brackets, for example (450)
For information only, worked out from other sizes; not toleranced and not worked to

blocks.note: If a needed size is missing, work it out from the sizes given, and check your answer against the overall size. **Do not scale** the drawing: prints are often reduced or enlarged. An A3 drawing printed on A4 is reduced to about 71%, so its scale is no longer the one in the title block.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The **scale** compares the size on the drawing with the real size. At 1:10, 1 mm on the drawing is 10 mm on the job; at 2:1 the drawing is twice full size.

ul: Real size = drawing size × the scale number. At 1:25, a member drawn 58 mm long is 58 × 25 = **1450 mm**.
Drawing size = real size ÷ the scale number. At 1:5, a 35 mm hole is drawn 35 ÷ 5 = **7 mm** across.

To choose a scale: divide the real size by the space on the sheet, then choose the next standard scale that is smaller. A 5.4 m beam in 200 mm of space: 5400 ÷ 200 = 27, so 1:25 is too big (216 mm) and **1:50** (108 mm) fits.
'NTS' means not to scale.

blocks.p: A **tolerance** is how far a real size may be from the drawn size and still be accepted. The **tolerance band** is the difference between the largest and the smallest sizes allowed.

head: How it is written
Largest
Smallest
Band
rows: General note: 'Fabrication tolerance ±2 mm unless stated'

blocks.p: When parts are joined end to end, their tolerances add up. Four parts, each 150 ± 0.3 mm, welded in a line can make a total anywhere from 598.8 mm to 601.2 mm, a spread of 2.4 mm, even though every part is good. This is why the designer may put a tighter tolerance on the overall size, why important sizes are measured from one datum, and why the fitter checks overall sizes during assembly, not only each part.

head: Section
Written as (example)
What the numbers mean
rows: Legs 100 mm and 75 mm, 8 mm thick
100 mm deep, 50 mm wide, 4 mm wall
Nominal bore 50 mm (2 in); 60.3 mm outside diameter; wall thickness set by the schedule
About 203 mm deep, about 133 mm wide, 25 kg per metre
About 152 mm deep and wide, 23 kg per metre

blocks.p: Steel used in Jamaica comes from several countries, so you will also see American sizes in inches: for example **W8 × 18** (a wide-flange beam about 8 in deep, weighing 18 lb per foot), **HSS 4 × 4 × 1/4** (a square hollow section 4 in square with a 1/4 in wall) and **C6 × 8.2** (a channel 6 in deep, 8.2 lb per foot). Never assume a metric section is the same as an imperial one that looks close.

ul: The drawing or specification gives the grade, for example S275 or S355 (European), or ASTM A36 for plate and sections and ASTM A500 for hollow sections (American).
Use the grade stated. A different grade, even a 'stronger' one, may weld differently or need a different procedure. Only the supervisor or engineer can approve a substitute, in writing.

head: On the drawing
Meaning
rows: Typical: the same at every similar place
Across flats (the size of a nut or hexagon)
1 off as drawn, 1 off opposite hand
Make one as drawn and one as its mirror image

ul: **'Hot-dip galvanise after fabrication':** all cutting, welding and drilling is finished first, then the whole item is dipped. Closed hollow sections need **vent and drain holes** where the drawing or galvaniser says, or trapped air and moisture can burst them in the hot zinc. Remove slag, spatter, oil and paint markings before it goes.
**'Remove all sharp edges' or 'break edges':** lightly deburr or chamfer every edge, so no one is cut.
**'Ø22 holes for M20 bolts':** clearance holes, bigger than the bolt so it fits.
**'6 × Ø14 EQ SP on 120 PCD':** six 14 mm holes, equally spaced on a 120 mm pitch circle.
**Hexagon sizes 'A/F':** measured across the flat faces, which is the spanner size.

blocks.note: Near the coast, the drawing may call for galvanising, stainless steel or a special paint system. Do not change the finish to save time or money: the designer chose it for how long the job must last in salt air.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Welds are shown on drawings by **weld symbols**. This section follows the AWS (American Welding Society) style, which you will often meet; check which system each drawing uses (see the ISO note at the end of this section).

blocks.h: The parts of a weld symbol

head: Part
Where it is
What it tells the welder
rows: Which joint is welded. The side the arrow touches is the **arrow side**.
The horizontal line joined to the arrow
Everything else is placed on it
Basic weld symbol below the line
Basic weld symbol above the line
To the left of the symbol
For a fillet, the leg size (6 = 6 mm leg)
To the right of the symbol
50-150 = welds 50 mm long at 150 mm centres; no length means the full length of the joint
The V at the end of the reference line
Extra information: process, procedure (WPS) number or a note
Where the arrow meets the reference line
Weld all the way round the joint
Where the arrow meets the reference line
Make this weld on site, not in the workshop
Flush (straight line), convex or concave, with a letter for the finishing method

head: Weld
Symbol looks like
Notes
rows: A right-angled triangle, upright side on the left
The most common symbol in fabrication
Square edges, often with a root opening
An upright line and a sloping line, like half a V
Only one member is bevelled: the arrow has a break (a bend) pointing at that member
A U, and half a U
J: the arrow break points at the member to be prepared
Weld through a hole or slot in one part
A run on the back of a groove weld
Two curves, or one line and one curve
Joints on rounded edges, such as bar or tube laid together

ul: The **root opening** (gap) is written inside the groove symbol: '2' inside a V means a 2 mm gap.
The **groove angle** is written beside the symbol, away from the reference line: 60° for an included angle of 60°.
The depth of preparation, and the weld's effective throat in brackets, are written to the left of the symbol.
**Pitch** is the distance from the centre of one weld to the centre of the next, not the gap between welds.

Unless the drawing says otherwise, there is a weld at each end of the joint. Number of welds = (joint length − weld length) ÷ pitch + 1. A 1240 mm joint with 40-200 welds: (1240 − 40) ÷ 200 + 1 = **7 welds**.
**Chain intermittent:** welds on both sides of the joint opposite each other (the two symbols line up).
**Staggered intermittent:** welds on both sides placed in between each other (the two symbols are offset along the reference line).

blocks.p: A flush contour line with G means grind the weld flush with the surface. A convex contour with no letter means leave the weld convex, as welded.

ul: Fillet triangle **below** the line, 6 on its left, nothing on its right: a 6 mm fillet on the arrow side, the full length of the joint.
Fillet triangles **above and below**, each with 5 and 50-150, lined up: 5 mm chain intermittent fillets on both sides.
Circle and flag at the arrow, fillet below, 6: a 6 mm fillet all round the joint, made on site.
Bevel symbol below the line with 45° beside it and 2 inside, the arrow broken towards the upright plate: bevel the upright plate at 45° on the arrow side, with a 2 mm root opening.

blocks.note: On drawings made to the ISO standard you may see a **dashed line** running beside the solid reference line. In that system a symbol on the solid line means the arrow side, and a symbol on the dashed line means the other side. ISO drawings also put a letter in front of a fillet size: **a5** means a 5 mm throat, **z7** a 7 mm leg. If you are not sure which system a drawing uses, ask before you weld.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **sketch** is a freehand drawing, made quickly but carefully, that shows the shape and sizes of something. Sketches pass information from a site or an existing part to the workshop, and help you plan before a drawing is made.

ul: Squared (grid) paper, or isometric grid paper, on a clipboard
HB and 2B pencils, an eraser
On site: steel tape, steel rule, square, spirit level, a phone or camera, and a second person to hold the tape
Draw light **construction lines** first, then go over the correct lines firmly.
Keep things in **proportion** by counting grid squares: if each square stands for 100 mm, a 1.2 m post is 12 squares long.
Sketch a circle by first drawing a light square box and its centre lines, then curving through the four mid-points.
Put sizes on after the outline is complete, with dimension lines, arrows and extension lines as on a drawing.
Add a title block: what it is, the job, your name, the date, 'NTS', and a sheet number.
Choose the front view that shows most about the shape; add a plan and an end view only if they are needed.
Keep the views lined up, in the projection your Centre uses, so each feature can be followed from view to view.
Dimension from clear datums, such as a floor level, a wall face or one end.
Draw the three **axes**: one upright, two at **30°** to the horizontal.
Sizes are measured **true length only along the axes** and lines parallel to them.
A sloping or diagonal line (a brace, a chamfer) is not true length: plot its two ends by measuring along the axes, then join them.
Circles become **ellipses**: draw the square box round the circle in isometric (a rhombus), then sketch the ellipse touching the middle of each side.
**Oblique** sketches are quicker for parts with round faces: draw the front face true shape, and the depth lines at 45°, usually at half length.

flow: Plan: the views needed, the tools, who measures and who records; check the area is safe
Look at the item and decide the datums (floor level, wall face, one end)
Sketch the outline of each view freehand, in proportion
Measure and write on the overall sizes first, then the details, from the datums
Note section sizes, material, holes, welds, fixings and their condition (rust, cracks, loose bolts)
Take photos with a tape in view, from several sides
Check: the parts add up to the overall sizes, and a second person re-measures the key sizes before you leave

blocks.note: On a sloping yard or uneven floor, do not measure heights from the ground at each post. Set up a **level datum line** with a spirit level and a straight edge, or a water level, and measure every height from it.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Method
Advantages
Limits
rows: Quick; needs only paper and pencil
Made on site while you look at the job
Can show sizes, hidden features and notes
Can be unclear, and sizes can be missed
Easy to change, copy and send
Can give cutting lists and weld symbols
Needs a computer, software and a trained person
Shows the real shape, condition and surroundings, such as rust or a pipe in the way
Gives no sizes unless a tape is in view
Can hide depth and distort shapes

blocks.p: A good job pack uses a dimensioned sketch or CAD drawing, backed up by photos.

flow: Check the drawing register: every sheet is there and each is the latest revision
Read each title block: number, revision, scale, projection, units, general tolerance
Read the revision table to see what has changed
Read every note: material, finish, weld notes, tolerances, standards
Compare the GA, the details and the parts list: part numbers, quantities and sizes agree
Check the sizes add up to the overall sizes
Look for clashes with the site and anything you do not understand
Send queries in writing before work starts

blocks.p: A mistake found on paper costs a phone call; the same mistake found after cutting and welding costs time, steel and the customer's trust.
Read the GA for every member, its part mark and quantity, then each detail for its section, material and end details. How the corners are made changes the cut lengths.
Example: a frame **1600 mm × 900 mm outside**, in 40 × 40 mm SHS.

head: Corner detail
Cut lengths
rows: Butt corners, top and bottom run full width
Butt corners, uprights run full height
2 uprights at 900 mm; 2 rails at 1600 − (2 × 40) = 1520 mm
2 at 1600 mm and 2 at 900 mm, measured along the outside edge, with 45° ends

ul: Add the saw cut allowance when working out how many pieces come from a stock length.
Total each section's length to order the material.
Have a second person check the cutting list against the drawing before anything is cut.

blocks.p: A **weld schedule** lists each joint with its weld type, size, side, length or pitch, and any site welds, read from the weld symbols. It lets the welders plan their work and the inspector check every joint.

For a tricky joint, set it out full size on a steel sheet or board from the drawing: the members, their angles, the weld preparation and the root gap. Lay the real pieces on it to check the fit before cutting the batch.

blocks.h: When the drawing and reality disagree

ul: **Parts list and GA disagree** (for example 4 off on the list, 6 shown): do not guess. Check with the drawing office or supervisor.
**The design clashes with the site** (for example a bracket where a pipe already runs): stop that part of the work, report it, and get the change in writing.
**Material is not as drawn** (different section or grade): use it only with written approval from the supervisor or engineer.
Record every answer on the working drawing, signed and dated.

blocks.h: Checking finished work against the drawing

ul: Measure the key sizes: overall length, width and height, hole positions, and the diagonals of frames.
Check weld sizes with a fillet gauge, and that every weld on the schedule has been made.
Compare each size with its tolerance, and record pass or fail on an inspection report with your name and the date.
Do not just look at it from a distance, or ask the welder whether it is right.

blocks.h: Briefing the team on a drawing

flow: Gather the team with the current drawing, parts list and job card
Show the title block: number, revision, scale, projection, units
Walk through the GA: overall sizes and how the parts fit together
Point out materials, finish and notes (for example galvanising near the sea)
Explain the weld symbols, site welds and key tolerances, and how they will be checked
Give each person their parts and tasks
Ask each person to explain back what they will make; invite questions

blocks.p: If a team member cannot follow a view or a section, show them the cutting plane on the drawing beside the real part, or a model, and let them find the features for themselves. Do not do it for them, and do not leave them to guess.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can name the main types of drawing and say who uses each.
I can read a title block and a revision table.
I can explain how drawings are controlled, and the team leader's part in it.
I can name the types of line and say what each shows.
I can tell first angle from third angle projection by the view positions and the symbol.
I can read a section view, its cutting plane and its hatching.
I can explain when an auxiliary view is used.
I can read datum, chain and reference dimensions, and explain why chain errors add up.
I can work with scales, both ways, and choose a scale to fit a sheet.
I can work out tolerance limits and bands, and how tolerances add up.
I can read steel section sizes, material grades, finishes and common abbreviations.
I can read a weld symbol: type, side, size, length and pitch, tail, all round, field weld and finish.
I can work out how many intermittent welds a joint needs.
I can make a neat, dimensioned freehand orthographic sketch and an isometric sketch.
I can sketch existing work on site and check my sketch.
I can produce a cutting list and a weld schedule from a drawing.
I can deal with errors and clashes on a drawing correctly.
I can check finished work against a drawing and record it.
I can brief a team on a drawing.

terms: Arrow side
The side of the joint the weld symbol's arrow touches
Auxiliary view
A view looking straight at a sloping face, to show its true shape
Bill of materials (BOM)
A list of every part with its material, size and quantity
Chain dimensioning
Sizes given from each feature to the next, so errors can add up
Cutting plane
A line showing where a section is taken; its arrows show the direction of viewing
Datum
The edge, line or point that sizes are measured from
Development
The flat shape of a sheet-metal part before it is bent or rolled
Dimension line
A thin line with arrowheads at each end that carries a size
Drawing register
A list of every drawing number with its latest revision
Field weld
A weld made on site; shown by a flag on the weld symbol
First angle projection
Each view drawn on the far side of the object from where it is seen
General arrangement (GA)
A drawing showing how all the parts of an item fit together
Hatching
Thin, evenly spaced lines drawn across a cut surface in a section
Isometric
A pictorial view with its axes at 30° to the horizontal
Other side
The side of the joint away from the arrow
Pitch (of welds)
The distance between the centres of intermittent welds
Reference dimension
A size in brackets, given for information only
Reference line
The horizontal line of a weld symbol that carries all its information
Revision
A numbered or lettered change to a drawing
Scale
The ratio of the size on the drawing to the real size
Section
A view drawn as if the part had been cut through
Third angle projection
Each view drawn on the same side of the object it is seen from
Title block
The panel giving the drawing's number, title, revision, scale and other details
Tolerance band
The difference between the largest and smallest sizes allowed
Weld schedule
A list of every joint with its weld type, size and side

c1.title: A bus-stop shelter in Annotto Bay
c1.text: Chevelle leads a team making steel bus-stop shelters for a municipal corporation job in Annotto Bay, St Mary. On Tuesday the office issues revision C of the shelter drawing; the team has been working from revision B, and some purlins and cleats are already cut. Chevelle also finds that a trainee has welded the end-plate cleats on the wrong face of two rafters. The projection symbol on the drawing shows the two circles beside the small end of the cone.

c2.title: Weld symbols on a hotel railing in Ocho Rios
c2.text: Akeem is preparing the weld schedule for a balcony railing at a hotel in Ocho Rios, St Ann. On the rail-to-post joints, fillet symbols appear above and below the reference line, each marked 5 and 40-200, with the lower symbol shifted along the line from the upper one. Each top rail joint is 1040 mm long. The base plate joints show a circle and a flag where the arrow meets the reference line. A butt joint in the posts shows a V symbol with '2' inside it.

c3.title: Sketching a market stall frame in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: Tamoy is sent to a market in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, to sketch a damaged steel stall frame so that a replacement can be made in the workshop. The frame has three equal bays, square tube posts, and a diagonal brace in each end bay. The market yard slopes, so the posts stand at different ground levels. Tamoy measures the overall length as 3640 mm.

c4.title: A display rack in Half Way Tree
c4.text: Jhanielle has a drawing at 1:10 for a display rack for a shop in Half Way Tree, St Andrew. The rack's frame is 1800 mm wide and 1200 mm high outside, in 40 × 40 mm SHS. The two uprights run full height, and three rails are fitted between them. The drawing was made on A3 paper but her copy has been printed on A4, and the size of one shelf cleat is missing.

c5.title: Briefing a gate team in Brown's Town
c5.text: Fitzroy is about to brief his team of four on a drawing for a pair of driveway gates for a house in Brown's Town, St Ann. The gate frames are closed rectangular hollow sections. The notes say 'HOT-DIP GALVANISE AFTER FABRICATION' and 'ALL WELDS 5 mm FILLET U.N.O.'.

questions.q: Before the team carries on, what should Chevelle check first in revision C?
o: The scale in the title block, to see whether the views have been drawn larger
The weld procedure, to see whether a different electrode is now needed
The revision table, to see if parts cut to revision B are affected
The parts list only, as a revision never changes the sizes of any parts
questions.why: The revision table says what changed. Chevelle must find out whether the purlins and cleats already cut to revision B still match, and keep any that do not apart.

questions.q: How can Chevelle find the changed areas on the revision C drawing itself?
o: Look for clouds or revision triangles drawn beside the changes
Look for the sizes printed in red, as all changes are coloured
Compare it line by line with revision B, as changes are not marked
Look in the tail of each weld symbol for the revision letter
questions.why: Drawing offices mark each change with a cloud (a wavy outline) or a small triangle holding the revision letter, matching the entry in the revision table.

questions.q: Which projection does the shelter drawing use?
o: First angle
Isometric projection
Oblique projection
Third angle
questions.why: In the projection symbol, the circles beside the small end of the cone mean third angle. Reading third angle views as first angle puts features on the wrong face, as happened with the cleats.

questions.q: What do the offset fillet symbols on the rail-to-post joints ask for?
o: 5 mm chain intermittent fillets on both sides
5 mm staggered intermittent fillets on both sides
5 mm continuous fillets on both sides of the joint
5 mm intermittent fillets on the arrow side only
questions.why: Symbols above and below the reference line mean both sides. When they are shifted along the line from each other, the welds on one side fall between those on the other: staggered intermittent.

questions.q: If there is a weld at each end, how many 40 mm welds are needed on one side of a 1040 mm top rail joint?
questions.why: The pitch of 200 mm is centre to centre. Number of welds = (1040 − 40) ÷ 200 + 1 = 6, with the first and last welds finishing at the ends of the joint.

questions.q: What does the circle with a flag on the base plate joints mean?
o: Weld all the way round the joint, in the shop
Grind the weld flush all round after welding
Inspect the weld on site with a flag test
Weld all the way round the joint, on site
questions.why: The circle at the junction of the arrow and reference line means weld all round; the flag means a field (site) weld. Base plates are often welded or fixed on site, after the posts are set.

questions.q: What does the '2' inside the V symbol tell the welder?
o: Leave a 2 mm root opening (gap) between the parts
Make the weld in two runs, one from each side
Bevel each edge to 2 mm before the parts are fitted
Use a 2 mm electrode or wire for the root run
questions.why: A figure written inside a groove symbol is the root opening. The groove angle is written beside the symbol, and the size of the preparation to its left.

questions.q: On her isometric sketch, how should Tamoy draw the diagonal braces?
o: Draw each brace at 30° and measure its true length along it
Draw each brace at 45°, as all braces are shown that way
Plot both ends by measuring along the axes, then join them
Leave the braces out, as diagonals cannot be shown in isometric
questions.why: Only lines parallel to the isometric axes are drawn true length. A diagonal is found from the positions of its two ends, measured along the axes, then joined.

questions.q: The posts stand at different ground levels. How should Tamoy measure their heights?
o: From the ground at the foot of each post, as each one stands
From the lowest post's base, measured with the tape leaning out
By counting the courses of a nearby block wall at each post
From one level datum line, set with a spirit or water level
questions.why: Measured from sloping ground, every post would seem a different height. A level datum line gives one reference for every height, so the new frame fits the real slope.

questions.q: Tamoy's three bay sizes add up to 3580 mm, but the overall length she measured is 3640 mm. What should she do before leaving?
o: Add the missing 60 mm to the middle bay, as it is most likely to be wrong
Re-measure the bays and the overall length with a second person
Use the overall length and let the workshop share the difference out
Use the three bay sizes, as small sizes are always more accurate
questions.why: Sizes that do not add up mean a measurement or a note is wrong. Re-measuring on site with a second person is quick; guessing in the workshop risks a frame that does not fit.

questions.q: How should Tamoy draw the round post caps on her isometric sketch?
o: As ellipses drawn inside isometric squares
As true circles drawn with a coin or compass
As squares, since circles cannot be shown
As half circles, showing the front half only
questions.why: A circle on any face of an isometric view appears as an ellipse. Sketch the square box round it in isometric first, then the ellipse touching the middle of each side.

questions.q: What is the cut length of each of the three rails?
questions.why: The rails fit between the two uprights, so each is the outside width less two tube widths: 1800 − (2 × 40) = 1720 mm. 1760 mm takes off only one tube width.

questions.q: How should Jhanielle find the size of the shelf cleat that is missing from her copy?
o: Measure it on the A4 copy and multiply the reading by ten
Measure it on the A4 copy and multiply the reading by twenty
Work it out from other sizes, or ask the drawing office
Copy the size of the cleat used on the last rack the shop made
questions.why: An A3 drawing printed on A4 is reduced to about 71%, so the 1:10 scale no longer holds. Never scale a print: work the size out from given sizes, or get it from the drawing office.

questions.q: What total length of 40 × 40 mm SHS goes on Jhanielle's cutting list for the frame?
questions.why: Two uprights at 1200 mm (2400 mm) and three rails at 1720 mm (5160 mm) make 7560 mm. 7800 mm uses the full 1800 mm for each rail.

questions.q: Because the gate frames are closed hollow sections, what must the team make sure of before galvanising?
o: Every closed section is sealed tight so no zinc can get inside
Vent and drain holes are made where the drawing says
Each frame is primed and painted so the zinc sticks better
The ends of each section are left open and unwelded
questions.why: In the hot zinc bath, air and moisture trapped in a sealed section expand and can burst it, and zinc must be able to flow in and out. Paint stops the zinc bonding to the steel.

questions.q: What does 'ALL WELDS 5 mm FILLET U.N.O.' mean?
o: Every weld is a 5 mm fillet unless the drawing notes another weld
Every weld is a 5 mm fillet, even where a different weld is shown
Every weld is 5 mm long, at the welder's own choice of spacing
Every weld is a 5 mm fillet unless the welder needs a larger one
questions.why: U.N.O. means unless noted otherwise. Any joint with its own weld symbol or note follows that; all the others get a 5 mm fillet.

questions.q: On a drawing of a bracket, a thin line made of long and short dashes runs through the middle of each hole. What does it show?
o: The centre line of the hole
A hidden edge behind the hole
Where a section is cut
A break in the bracket
questions.why: Thin chain lines (long dash, short dash) mark centre lines, lines of symmetry and pitch circles. Hidden edges are short dashes, and cutting planes have thick ends with arrows.

questions.q: In a section view of a bolted joint, the plates are hatched but the bolt, cut along its length, is not. Why?
o: The bolt was missed out by mistake and should have been hatched as well
Only parts made of mild steel are hatched, and bolts are a harder steel
By convention, bolts cut along their length are not hatched
Bolts are always drawn in a separate view, so their hatching is left off
questions.why: By convention, bolts, nuts, pins, shafts and thin ribs cut along their length are left unhatched, so they stand out clearly from the parts they join.

questions.q: A parts list calls for 'CHS 48.3 × 3.2'. What is it?
o: Round tube, 48.3 mm inside diameter, 3.2 m long
Square tube, 48.3 mm across, 3.2 mm wall thickness
Round bar, 48.3 mm diameter, 3.2 kg per metre
Round tube, 48.3 mm outside diameter, 3.2 mm wall
questions.why: CHS is circular hollow section: round tube, given as outside diameter × wall thickness. 48.3 mm is a common size for handrails and scaffold tube.

questions.q: Which of these is written correctly for a parallel flange channel 150 mm deep with 75 mm wide flanges?
questions.why: PFC stands for parallel flange channel, given as depth × flange width. RHS is a rectangular tube, L is an angle and UB is a universal beam.
